individual_reviews.label: reviewer_1

review.Summary: The paper presents MotionStream, a streaming motion-conditioned video generation framework that distills a bidirectional motion-controlled teacher diffusion model into a causal autoregressive student using Self Forcing-style DMD with attention sinks and rolling KV cache. It introduces a lightweight sinusoidal track embedding head, joint text-motion classifier-free guidance, and a tiny VAE decoder to achieve up to 29 FPS with sub-second latency on a single H100, enabling interactive drag, camera, and motion-transfer control over long/infinite videos. Experiments on DAVIS, Sora subset, and LLFF show competitive or SOTA quality/motion adherence with much higher throughput.
Strengths: Real-time interactive video generation with constant latency is a substantial practical advance over offline diffusion methods.
The attention-sink plus rolling KV cache with self-rollout training is a well-motivated and thorough solution to long-horizon drift.
The lightweight PE track representation and joint text-motion guidance improve both efficiency and motion fidelity, with extensive ablations supporting design choices.
Broad applicability is demonstrated across drag, camera control, and motion transfer, with quantitative gains on DAVIS/Sora and LLFF while being over an order of magnitude faster.
The paper clearly discloses limitations, reproducibility details, and training hyperparameters.
Weaknesses: Quantitative evaluation relies mainly on reconstruction-style metrics on limited benchmarks; the user study only assesses quality, not controllability, and VBench results show weak discriminative power.

Baselines use very different backbones and resolutions (e.g., ATI 14B vs 1.3B), so 'state-of-the-art' claims may be confounded by backbone capacity; no controlled same-backbone comparisons are provided.
Infinite-length streaming is demonstrated only up to 241 frames; behavior beyond this remains unverified.
The causal student degrades motion accuracy (EPE) compared to the teacher, but the trade-off between speed and controllability is not deeply analyzed.
The paper lacks detailed memory/VRAM usage analysis and does not clarify how online user edits to trajectories are reconciled with already-generated video chunks.
Questions: How does MotionStream compare to CausVid or TalkingMachines under the same backbone and evaluation protocol? Are the gains primarily from attention sinks and self-rollout training?
What is the exact FPS measurement protocol? Does it include VAE decoding, and is it measured per generated chunk (3 frames) or per full video?
How does the model behave beyond 241 frames? Are there any experiments at 500+ frames to support the 'infinite-length' claim?
In the user study, only video quality was assessed. Were participants asked about trajectory adherence or interactivity? If not, why?
What is the peak GPU memory usage during streaming inference for Wan 2.1-1.3B and Wan 2.2-5B?

When a user modifies a trajectory mid-stream, how does the model handle the fact that previously generated frames were conditioned on old trajectory inputs? Does it retroactively update or just follow the new control for future chunks?
How sensitive is the method to the choice of CoTracker3 for extracting tracks versus manually drawn tracks? Is there a domain gap?
Limitations: Extrapolation is only tested up to 241 frames; true infinite-length behavior remains unverified.
The fixed attention sink constrains scenarios with complete scene changes, as acknowledged by the authors.
Rapid or physically implausible trajectories cause artifacts; complex scenes and multiple identities can lead to identity loss or deformation.
Training requires 32 GPUs and a substantial synthetic data pipeline, which may limit reproducibility for many research groups.
Potential misuse for creating deceptive media is inherent to video generation, though an ethics statement is provided.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_2

review.Summary: MotionStream proposes a streaming motion-conditioned video generation framework. It first trains a bidirectional motion-guided teacher (Wan DiT) using sinusoidal track embeddings and joint text-motion classifier-free guidance, then distills it into a causal autoregressive student via Self-Forcing-style distribution matching distillation. The student uses sliding-window causal attention with attention sinks and rolling KV caches to enable constant-latency, indefinite-length generation at up to 29 FPS on a single GPU. The method is evaluated on motion transfer, novel view synthesis, and long-video extrapolation, with ablations on track encoding, guidance, attention patterns, and a Tiny VAE decoder.
Strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: real-time interactive motion-controlled video generation, which prior diffusion-based methods cannot handle due to latency and non-causality.

Novel combination of attention sinks, rolling KV caches, and self-rollout training for video diffusion, effectively bridging the train-test gap for autoregressive extrapolation and improving long-video stability.
Lightweight track representation (sinusoidal PE + track head) is faster and better than RGB-VAE encoding, and joint text-motion guidance improves realism without sacrificing trajectory adherence.

Strong empirical results: outperforms offline baselines on DAVIS/Sora motion transfer and LLFF novel view synthesis while being 20-70x faster, and the distilled causal model retains most of the teacher's quality.
Detailed ablation studies and practical engineering (Tiny VAE, streaming demo) support the design choices and demonstrate real-time interaction capabilities.
Clear writing and sufficient training/inference details for reproducibility, including hyperparameters, data preprocessing, and evaluation protocols.
Weaknesses: No quantitative comparison to prior autoregressive/streaming video diffusion baselines (e.g., CausVid, Self-Forcing, TalkingMachines) on standard benchmarks; only offline bidirectional baselines are compared, making the claimed advantages less clear.

The 'infinite-length' claim is not fully substantiated: extrapolation is only tested up to ~241 frames, and no evidence is provided for much longer horizons or constant-latency behavior over thousands of frames.

The evaluation metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/EPE) are reconstruction-oriented and may not capture interactive experience quality; user study only assesses static quality, not controllability or interactivity.

End-to-end interaction latency is not clearly measured; the reported FPS focuses on generation, while track extraction (e.g., CoTracker3) and user input processing may add overhead in a real interactive loop.
Some details of DMD distillation are underspecified, such as the exact fake score training loss, the choice of timestep distribution, and sensitivity to the 1:5 update ratio and gradient truncation.

Training requires substantial compute (32 A100 GPUs for days) and large synthetic datasets, limiting reproducibility; the method's robustness to noisy/imperfect user trajectories remains only partially addressed by stochastic masking.
Questions: How does MotionStream quantitatively compare to CausVid, Self-Forcing, and TalkingMachines on long-video generation benchmarks (e.g., time-averaged LPIPS, EPE, throughput) for both fixed-length and extrapolated settings?
What is the actual maximum length tested, and does the latency/quality remain truly constant for, say, 10,000+ frames? Are there any signs of drift beyond 241 frames?
What is the end-to-end interactive latency including user input processing, track extraction/update, and rendering? How much does track extraction with CoTracker3 add to the reaction time?
Why is chunk size 3 optimal? Did the authors train models with different chunk sizes, or is this chosen only from inference-time evaluation?

How robust is the method to track occlusions and object disappearance? Does stochastic masking fully address the ambiguity between occluded and unspecified tracks, and are there quantitative artifact measures?

Since the teacher uses joint CFG with 3 NFE, does the distilled student (with 1 NFE) fully preserve both text and motion conditioning? Is there a measurable drop in text-alignment (e.g., VBench text metrics) compared to the teacher?
How sensitive is DMD distillation to the fake-score update ratio (1:5) and gradient truncation? What happens with 1:1 or 1:10 ratios?
Limitations: The fixed attention sink anchors the initial scene, causing the model to preserve the starting environment rather than adapting to complete scene changes, as the authors acknowledge.
Extremely rapid or physically implausible trajectories can cause temporal inconsistencies and object distortions.
The model struggles with highly complex scenes or multiple subjects, sometimes losing identity information and producing artifacts.
User-drawn imperfect trajectories (e.g., flat grids) can degrade quality; stochastic masking only partially mitigates this, and the model's robustness to noisy inputs is not deeply analyzed.
The 'infinite-length' claim is not fully verified; experiments only go to ~241 frames, and behavior on much longer horizons remains unknown.
Training resource requirements are high (32 A100 GPUs, synthetic data from large models), which may hinder reproducibility and adoption in resource-constrained settings.
The evaluation focuses on reconstruction-based metrics and static quality; the interactive experience itself is not rigorously evaluated.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_3

review.Summary: MotionStream presents a streaming motion-conditioned video generation framework. It first augments a Wan-based text-to-video diffusion model with motion control using sinusoidal track embeddings and joint text-motion guidance, resulting in a bidirectional teacher. This teacher is then distilled into a causal few-step student via Self Forcing-style distribution matching distillation, with sliding-window causal attention, attention sinks, and rolling KV caches simulated during training. The paper reports real-time throughput (up to 29.5 FPS with a custom tiny VAE) and favorable motion-following metrics on DAVIS/Sora motion transfer and LLFF novel-view synthesis, positioning the method as enabling interactive infinite-length video generation.
Strengths: Real-time streaming generation with motion control is an important and timely capability; the paper demonstrates substantial speed improvements over offline diffusion baselines.

The attention-sink and rolling KV cache design, combined with train-time self-rollout to close the train-inference gap, is a sensible and well-motivated solution for stable long-horizon autoregressive video diffusion.
The lightweight sinusoidal track embedding with a learnable track head is shown to be faster and more accurate than RGB/VAE-based encoding in their ablation.
Joint text-motion guidance appears to balance trajectory adherence with natural dynamics, and the guidance-weight ablation provides useful insight.
The authors include detailed implementation specifics and an honest appendix discussion of limitations and failure cases.
Weaknesses: The quantitative evaluation does not fully support the 'state-of-the-art' claim: comparisons use baselines with different backbone scales, resolutions, track representations, and evaluation protocols, making the numbers not directly comparable.

The closest prior autoregressive video-diffusion methods (CausVid, TalkingMachines, Self Forcing) are not quantitatively compared on the same benchmarks, so the claimed advantage over them is unsubstantiated.
The 'infinite-length' claim is only tested on sequences up to 241 frames; there is no evidence of stable generation for much longer horizons or adaptation to global scene changes.

The user study in the appendix shows that ATI (with a 14B backbone) is generally preferred for visual quality, which weakens the paper's assertion of state-of-the-art video quality independent of speed.

Distillation uses only synthetic data (a few thousand samples for causal adaptation and a few hundred steps for DMD), so generalization to open-domain real videos or arbitrary user trajectories remains unclear.

No evaluation of the interactive experience itself (e.g., user edits during generation, latency under changing control inputs) is reported; FPS and latency are measured in an offline generation setting.
Questions: Can you provide a head-to-head comparison with CausVid and TalkingMachines on the same motion-transfer and long-video benchmarks, ideally with controlled backbone and evaluation protocol?
How do the metrics change if all methods are re-evaluated with the same track extraction (e.g., CoTracker3 50x50 grid), the same first frame, text prompt, and resolution?

Have you tested generation beyond 241 frames (e.g., 1,000+ frames)? What is the maximum stable generation length, and does the rollout remain stable if the scene undergoes a complete global transition?
When a user adds, removes, or modifies tracks during streaming, how is the KV cache updated? Is there any quantitative or qualitative evaluation of mid-generation motion edits?
What is the memory footprint of the rolling KV cache, and how does it scale with chunk size and window size? Do the reported FPS numbers include the tiny VAE decoding cost?
Does the DMD distillation require the teacher to be evaluated on the full generated sequence, and what is the total training/GPU cost for the full pipeline?
Limitations: The infinite-length claim is supported only up to 241 frames; true unbounded generation is not demonstrated.
Fixed attention sinking anchors the model to the initial scene, which can cause drift or inability to adapt to large scene changes.
The evaluation is confounded by inconsistent baselines (different backbones, resolutions, and track-conditioning formats), making it hard to isolate the contribution of the proposed method.
The closest autoregressive video-diffusion baselines are not quantitatively compared, so relative advantages remain unclear.
Distillation training uses only synthetic data, which may limit robustness on real-world open-domain inputs.
Real-time speeds are measured on a single H100 GPU; consumer-grade hardware performance is unknown.
Potential misuse of realistic generated video content warrants ethics review, though the paper includes an ethics statement.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_4

review.Summary: The paper presents MotionStream, a framework for interactive, real-time motion-conditioned video generation. It builds a motion-conditioned teacher model using lightweight sinusoidal track embeddings and joint text-motion guidance, then distills it into a causal autoregressive student using Self Forcing with DMD. Key innovations include attention sinks and rolling KV caches for constant-memory long-video generation, and a tiny VAE for decoding speed. The method achieves up to 29 FPS on a single H100 GPU and demonstrates SOTA results in motion transfer and camera control tasks.
Strengths: Novel system for real-time interactive video generation with motion control, addressing latency and causality issues that preclude interaction in prior diffusion-based methods.
Efficient track representation using sinusoidal embeddings with a learnable head, which is 40x faster than RGB-VAE and improves quality.
Joint text-motion guidance balances trajectory adherence with natural dynamics, leading to better qualitative results.
Attention sinking with rolling KV cache is a novel and effective mechanism for stable long-video extrapolation, as demonstrated by ablations.
Achieves two orders of magnitude speedup over prior motion-controlled video generation methods, with SOTA or competitive results on motion transfer and camera control.
Thorough ablations of chunk size, attention sink, window size, and guidance weights, with clear analysis of trade-offs.
Weaknesses: The 'infinite-length streaming' claim is only validated up to ~15 seconds (241 frames); longer-term stability is not demonstrated.

Evaluation of motion transfer relies on reconstruction metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, EPE) that may not capture perceptual quality; user study shows a larger backbone (ATI) is preferred for quality despite worse trajectory adherence.
The tiny VAE introduces quality degradation (LPIPS worsens) and may limit high-fidelity use cases; the trade-off is reported as marginal, but the evidence suggests a noticeable perceptual drop.
Distillation is performed only on synthetic data, which might limit generalization to real-world videos; the teacher itself is trained on a mix, but the student's training distribution is narrower.

Some implementation details are unclear, e.g., how the model handles user edits to tracks in real time, how the attention mask is implemented without explicit masking in training, and how the KV cache is managed across chunks.

Baselines are not optimized for streaming, so the FPS comparisons, while impressive, are somewhat expected; a fairer comparison would involve adapting baselines to causal inference or using latency-controlled settings.
Questions: Does the model maintain quality and latency for videos beyond 241 frames (e.g., minutes)? What is the empirical limit of the attention sink mechanism?

How are user-specified track modifications (e.g., dragging points to a new location) incorporated during live streaming? Does the model need to re-generate from the modification point or can it adapt in-place?
The paper states that no explicit attention masking is used; how exactly is the causal constraint enforced during training and inference with the rolling KV cache?
Why does a larger attention window degrade performance? Is this due to error accumulation in context tokens or due to positional encoding issues?
How is the joint guidance applied to the critic (fake score) during DMD distillation? The paper says no CFG is applied to the fake score, but does the critic see both text and motion conditions?
What is the memory footprint and KV cache size for generating very long videos? Does it remain constant regardless of video length?
Limitations: The method struggles with complete scene changes and environments that evolve drastically, as the attention sink anchors to the initial chunk.
Extremely rapid or physically implausible trajectories cause artifacts and temporal inconsistencies.
Complex scenes with multiple objects or identities may lead to identity loss and quality degradation, partly due to backbone capacity.
The reliance on 2D tracks limits control over 3D motions and occlusions; the model cannot distinguish occluded tracks from unspecified tracks without the stochastic masking trick.
The fixed context window of one chunk may limit the model's ability to maintain long-term dependencies beyond immediate context.
Potential negative societal impact: the technology enables creation of deceptive media, requiring safeguards like watermarking and controlled access.

review.Summary: The paper proposes MotionStream, a method for real-time, streaming motion-conditioned video generation. It first trains a bidirectional motion-controlled teacher on Wan I2V models using sinusoidal track embeddings and joint text-motion guidance, then distills it into a causal autoregressive student via Self Forcing-style DMD with sliding-window attention, attention sinks, and rolling KV caches. The result is up to 29 FPS on a single H100 GPU with roughly constant latency for long videos. Experiments cover motion transfer, camera control, and ablations of key design choices.
Strengths: Achieves dramatic speedups (orders of magnitude) over offline motion-conditioned diffusion baselines while retaining competitive motion-following quality, enabling real-time interactive use.

The combination of attention sinks with rolling KV caches and simulating this setup during training is a sensible way to bridge the train-test distribution for long autoregressive extrapolation; the ablation supports the necessity of sinks.
The lightweight sinusoidal PE track head is faster and better than RGB-VAE encoding, and the joint text-motion guidance improves naturalness while preserving trajectory adherence.
Demonstrates downstream generality including drag control, camera control, and motion transfer, and works with both 1.3B and 5B backbones on a single GPU.
Comprehensive ablations on chunk size, sink size, window size, and sampling steps provide useful engineering insights.
Weaknesses: The 'infinite-length' claim is overclaimed: the fixed initial-frame sink anchors generation to the initial scene and cannot handle full scene changes or transitions; the paper acknowledges this but still markets infinite streams.

Quantitative comparisons are confounded by backbone and resolution differences; speed comparisons against unoptimized baselines are not apples-to-apples, and visual quality is heavily determined by the base model.

The distilled causal student degrades motion-following accuracy (EPE) and perceptual quality relative to the teacher, yet the paper's headline emphasizes state-of-the-art without fully discussing this trade-off.

Evaluation focuses on reconstruction (DAVIS/Sora) and novel-view synthesis; there are no large-scale user studies over longer horizons or open-ended interaction, and no direct comparison to CausVid or Self Forcing baselines.
Details of DMD/self-forcing training, such as critic conditioning, gradient truncation, and RoPE cache positions, are only partially specified, making reproduction challenging.
Questions: Can the model continue generating coherently after a complete scene change or cut, or does the fixed attention sink force the video to remain anchored to the initial frame indefinitely?
How was the critic/fake score function conditioned on text and motion, and does its objective include CFG? Please provide more training details for reproducibility.
What is the exact memory footprint and KV-cache size as a function of video length, and does the Tiny VAE or any other component grow with sequence length?
Why not include CausVid and Self Forcing as direct baseline comparisons in the tables, and how do the proposed sink/window designs compare quantitatively with full-context causal attention?
How robust is the method to user-drawn noisy or sparse trajectories; can quantitative results be provided for simulated imperfect tracks?
Limitations: Fixed initial-frame attention sink prevents adaptation to complete scene changes, limiting true open-ended 'infinite' generation.
Rapid or physically implausible motion creates artifacts; complex scenes with multiple identities can cause identity loss.
The student model underperforms its teacher in tracking precision (EPE) and perceptual quality; distillation introduces a quality-speed trade-off.
Evaluation is limited to short clips (81-241 frames) and reconstruction-style metrics; long-term semantic drift and open-domain interactivity are not fully measured.
Potential misuse for creating deceptive media is acknowledged but no concrete safeguards are provided.

review.Summary: MotionStream proposes a streaming motion-conditioned video generation framework that first trains a bidirectional motion-guided teacher using lightweight sinusoidal track embeddings and joint text-motion classifier-free guidance, then distills it into a causal autoregressive student via Self-Forcing-style distribution matching distillation. The student uses sliding-window causal attention with attention sinks and rolling KV caches to enable constant-latency, indefinite-length generation at up to 29 FPS on a single H100 GPU. The method is evaluated on motion transfer, camera control, and long-video extrapolation, with extensive ablations on design choices.
Strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: real-time interactive motion-conditioned video generation, which prior offline diffusion methods cannot support due to high latency and non-causality.

The combination of attention sinks, rolling KV caches, and self-rollout training is a well-motivated and effective solution to bridge the train-inference gap for stable long-horizon autoregressive video diffusion.
The lightweight sinusoidal track embedding with a learnable head is substantially faster and more accurate than RGB/VAE-based encoding, as demonstrated in ablations.
Joint text-motion guidance improves naturalness while preserving trajectory adherence, and the guidance-weight ablation provides useful insight.

Achieves orders-of-magnitude speedups (20-70x) over offline baselines while maintaining competitive motion-following quality on DAVIS/Sora and LLFF, with clear ablation studies supporting the design choices.
The paper provides detailed implementation specifics, hyperparameters, and honest disclosure of limitations, aiding reproducibility.
Weaknesses: The 'infinite-length' claim is overclaimed: experiments only go up to ~241 frames, and the fixed attention sink anchors generation to the initial scene, preventing adaptation to complete scene changes or transitions.

Quantitative comparisons are confounded by different backbone scales, resolutions, and track representations across baselines; no head-to-head comparison with prior autoregressive/streaming video-diffusion methods (e.g., CausVid, Self Forcing, TalkingMachines) is provided, so the claimed advantages over them are unsubstantiated.

Evaluation relies heavily on reconstruction-based metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, EPE) that may not capture interactive experience quality; the user study only assesses static visual quality and shows a larger-backbone baseline is preferred, and controllability/interactivity is not evaluated.

The distilled student degrades motion accuracy (EPE) and perceptual quality relative to the teacher, yet the paper's headline emphasizes state-of-the-art without deeply analyzing this speed-quality trade-off.

Training requires substantial compute (32 A100 GPUs) and synthetic data, which may limit reproducibility and robustness on open-domain real-world inputs; the method's sensitivity to noisy/imperfect user trajectories is only partially addressed.

Several implementation details are underspecified, including the exact DMD critic conditioning and loss, KV cache management for mid-stream user edits, and the end-to-end latency including track extraction and rendering.
Questions: How does MotionStream quantitatively compare to CausVid, Self Forcing, and TalkingMachines on the same benchmarks with controlled backbone and evaluation protocol?
What is the empirical maximum stable generation length, and does latency/quality remain constant for videos beyond 241 frames (e.g., 1,000+ frames)?
How are user-specified track modifications (e.g., dragging points to a new location) incorporated during live streaming? Does the model re-generate from the modification point or adapt in-place?
What is the exact end-to-end interactive latency including track extraction (e.g., CoTracker3) and rendering, and what is the peak GPU memory usage during streaming?
Why does a larger attention window degrade performance, and how exactly is the causal constraint enforced during training and inference with rolling KV caches?
How robust is the method to noisy or sparse user-drawn trajectories, and does stochastic masking fully address ambiguity between occluded and unspecified tracks?
Does the distilled student preserve text-alignment compared to the teacher, and what is the sensitivity of DMD distillation to the update ratio (1:5) and gradient truncation?
Limitations: The infinite-length claim is only supported up to ~241 frames; true unbounded generation is not demonstrated.
The fixed attention sink anchors generation to the initial scene, limiting adaptation to complete scene changes or global transitions.
Rapid or physically implausible trajectories can cause temporal inconsistencies and object distortions; complex scenes with multiple identities may lead to identity loss.
Evaluation is limited to short clips and reconstruction-style metrics; long-horizon semantic drift and open-domain interactivity are not fully measured.
Training requires 32 A100 GPUs and a substantial synthetic data pipeline, which may hinder reproducibility and adoption in resource-constrained settings.
The method relies on 2D tracks, which limits control over 3D motions and occlusions; the model cannot distinguish occluded tracks from unspecified tracks without stochastic masking.
Potential misuse of realistic generated video content is inherent; the paper includes an ethics statement but no concrete safeguards.
